t800.name: T-800
t800.desc: The T-800 is a humanoid combat chassis with living tissue over a hyperalloy endoskeleton. It possesses superhuman strength, advanced AI, and can pass as human.

subcats.name: HUMANOID LOCOMOTION
subcats.desc: Not just lab parkour — Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games (2025 & 2026) put hundreds of humanoids through track, hurdles, relays, football, and factory scenarios. Record times keep falling. Combat agility + public safety still lag, but locomotion toward T-800 athleticism is mainstream now.

subcats.name: LIVING TISSUE SKIN
subcats.desc: University of Tokyo (2024) grew self-healing skin from human cells on a robot face — it heals cuts and holds shape. Still lab-scale, not full-body. No sweat glands, hair follicles, or blood yet.

subcats.name: HUMAN-PASSING APPEARANCE
subcats.desc: Deepfake faces and AI voice cloning can fool humans in video calls. Physical robots like Ameca show expressive faces. Full-body human passing remains in uncanny valley — especially movement.

subcats.name: SUPERHUMAN STRENGTH
subcats.desc: Hydraulic robots exceed human strength. Boston Dynamics Atlas lifts 25kg overhead. Industrial arms lift 2,300kg. But nothing in a human-sized frame matching T-800's 400kg+ capability.

subcats.name: ONBOARD AI & DECISION MAKING
subcats.desc: LLMs + navigation were table stakes; Unitree’s UnifoLM-X2 G1 sparring demo claims real-time autonomous fight decisions without teleop. Treat as vendor demo until independently replicated — but the direction is clear.

subcats.name: POWER SOURCE
subcats.desc: T-800 runs on twin hydrogen fuel cells lasting 120 years. Current humanoids last 1-4 hours on lithium batteries. Miniature nuclear batteries (BV100) exist but produce microwatts. Biggest gap.

headlines.html: As the military speeds up the use of drones and AI in warfare, Congress considers safeguards (WUNC American Homefront Project, Jay Price, 8 Oct 2026) Per the report, at a Fort Bragg demonstration "Atop the cabs of two of the trucks were 12-gauge shotguns on robotic pivots, controlled by AI." The soldiers in charge said a human was "on the loop". The report says the committee added provisions to the pending annual military policy and spending bill that "would require human oversight of AI-controlled weapons, ban the use of AI for nuclear launch or detonation, and bar its use for domestic surveillance." CNAS's Paul Scharre: "So maybe a human is authorizing a target list of a whole bunch of targets, but the human doesn't really have time to pore through each one individually and analyze it." (WUNC American Homefront Project)

headlines.html: Army’s new command plans to streamline autonomous warfare acquisition (Defense One, Meghann Myers, 9 Oct 2026, 02:44am ET) Per Defense One, the Army has announced a Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM), to be led by an acquisition executive, which could nest under the new Autonomous Warfare Command. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle's memo calls for designating a Portfolio Acquisition Executive for autonomy. CSIS fellow Kateryna Bondar: "So I would say that autonomy that is being deployed right now, it's not some super sophisticated technology, AI-enabled full autonomy, or anything like that." On efforts to train agents: "if this agent is able to act and activate whatever effectors we have—be it missiles, be it drones, whatever it can employ—then the decision-making system and this agent can actually be called a weapon system." Per Defense One, the push "is not about robot drones finding, fixing, and deploying their weapons at will—at least not yet." (Defense One)

headlines.html: 2026 Usage Policy update (Anthropic, 8 Oct 2026) Anthropic's annual Usage Policy refresh. On weapons: "Recently, we’ve seen people attempt to use our models to build guidance and control software for weapons. The updated section makes clear that our prohibitions include the software and components that make weapons work, as well as actions like arming drones and other autonomous vehicles." For models connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and might be capable of causing injury: "A qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed; the equipment must also be able to hold a safe state if Claude is disconnected." Company policy; enforcement is by Anthropic. (Anthropic)

headlines.html: GA-ASI, US Navy Test Autonomous Mission Planning With MQ-20 Avenger (The Defense Post, Giulia Bernacchi, 8 Oct 2026) "General Atomics Aeronautical Systems (GA-ASI) and the US Navy have tested mission planning software that enables uncrewed aircraft to interpret a commander’s orders, coordinate with other aircraft, and adapt as threats change." "TacACE then used that information to interpret the commander’s intent and determine how to carry out the mission within those limits." "According to GA-ASI, the software coordinated crewed and uncrewed participants and adjusted the plan in real-time as the simulated combat scenario changed." Per The Defense Post, the MQ-20 flew from Gray Butte, California, in a live, virtual and constructive exercise with simulated participants and threats, and the team also evaluated how human operators interacted with the software. A company-reported test against simulated threats. (The Defense Post)

headlines.html: Shield AI expects to fly its unmanned fighter jet within months (Defense One, 8 Oct 2026, 4:15pm ET) "Shield AI expects to start flying its X-BAT prototype unmanned fighter jet by year’s end—and is getting $150 million from the Navy to keep developing it, officials said." Armor Harris, Shield AI's SVP of aircraft: "We've been building two prototype vehicles—they're full scale. The first one will be done in the next couple of weeks here." Per Defense One, the money is a milestone-based modification to an other transaction agreement, Shield AI will match it, and total planned development spending reaches $400 million, "all leading up to fielding an early operational capability in about 2029." Company and Navy plans; the jet has not flown yet. (Defense One)

headlines.html: CSG joins development of autonomous SwarmShot counter-UAS system (CSG release, Business Wire 7 Oct 2026) Federal Ammunition (CSG), Mossberg and Palladyne AI are jointly developing SwarmShot: drones fitted with a Mossberg airborne weapon module and Federal counter-drone shotshell ammunition, acting as reusable interceptors in a coordinated swarm. It starts as an add-on for Palladyne's Gremlin-X quadcopter mini-bomber. Per the release: "IntelliSwarm is designed to receive validated threat tracks from existing sensors or command systems to autonomously allocate targets among available interceptors, calculate intercept paths, maneuver each aircraft into an effective engagement position and redirect the swarm as targets move or new threats appear." Mossberg's Doug Bell: "This is not simply an existing shotgun mounted to a drone." On Palladyne's earlier Army swarm exercises, the release says "The aircraft operated collaboratively at the edge while soldiers retained authority over weapons employment." These are company plans; no schedules or customers were disclosed. (CSG)

headlines.html: Dutch firm uses AI to help drone systems ‘talk’ on Ukraine’s battlefield (Reuters via Defense News, 8 Oct 2026) In a late-September test at a Dutch airbase, Intelic's AI-powered Nexus software fused radars, sensors and cameras, used drone image recognition to verify a mock enemy drone, and launched an AI-guided interceptor. Per Reuters: "Although a human made the final decision to launch the AI-guided interceptor drone, the process could be fully autonomous, said Intelic CEO and founder Maurits Korthals Altes." On high-speed threats, Korthals Altes said "you’re not so likely to hit it manually, and you need a more autonomous system." Per Reuters, "Intelic’s command-and-control system is being rolled out on Ukraine’s battlefield." Intelic holds a €30m contract with the Dutch Defence Ministry. In this test a human made the launch decision. (Reuters via Defense News)

headlines.html: Shield AI and Innovaero collaborate on sovereign, autonomous loitering munitions for Australia (Shield AI press release, 6 Oct 2026) Under an MoU, Shield AI will put its Hivemind mission-autonomy software on Australian firm Innovaero's One-Way Loitering (OWL) munitions for the ADF. Per the release: "OWL munitions are designed to efficiently identify, track and strike targets." and "Hivemind will enable faster mission planning and increased lethality in OWL’s attacks." Hivemind is already integrated on the OWL-B ahead of flight testing, and "Multi-agent coordinated strike missions are being simulated in dynamic conditions with commands issued through the Android Team Awareness Kit (ATAK) tactical interface." Company claims; an MoU, with flight testing still to come. (Shield AI)

headlines.html: Harmattan AI unveils IRIFI autonomous strike system designed to hit human-approved targets at ranges of up to 2,000 km (Defence Industry Europe, 8 Oct 2026) French firm Harmattan AI has unveiled IRIFI, an autonomous deep-strike system with a range of up to 2,000 km. Per the report: "The system is intended to complete an authorised mission without human control after launch, within limits set by its commander." Commanders approve targets and set parameters before launch. The company says a single commander could direct dozens of autonomous strikes with an AI system processing satellite imagery, and that the design is meant for coordinated saturation strikes. CEO Mouad M’Ghari: "AI-powered autonomy now makes it possible to combine the best of both worlds, and that is exactly what we did with IRIFI." Company claims; no deployment or customer reported. (Defence Industry Europe)

headlines.html: Inside the U.S. 'kill chain' that destroyed an Iranian school (Bloomberg via Los Angeles Times, 21 Sep 2026; backfill, added 8 Oct) Per Bloomberg, officials involved in an internal Pentagon probe of the 28 Feb Tomahawk strike on a school in Minab, Iran, which killed at least 123 children, describe "a cascade of preventable failures." Compressed targeting timelines, "combined with gaps in underlying information about the site, cuts in civilian protection personnel and an overreliance on artificial intelligence technology — set the stage for the deadly error." "Inside Centcom, which conducted the U.S. attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System, the officials said." Palantir says it "is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies" and that there's no evidence its software was at fault. (Los Angeles Times (Bloomberg))

headlines.html: 🪖 Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools months after blacklisting company, BBC told (BBC, 5 Oct 2026) "The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday." "Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran." (sic) Earlier this year the Pentagon pressed Anthropic to remove Claude's safety guardrails: "When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk"." Claude was embedded in Palantir's Maven Smart System. Georgetown CSET's Lauren Kahn: "The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play." The Pentagon has since signed deals with Google, xAI and OpenAI. (BBC News)

headlines.html: UIUC's InterEvolve Lifts Unitree G1 Task Success From 8% to 86.5% (2 Oct 2026): Goal-conditioned humanoid task success rose from 8% with human-written rewards to 86.5% after test-time evolution, at 2.1 GPU-hours per task. "A large language model (LLM) agent revises the program structure in context, drawing on execution feedback and a skill library of verified programs," the authors write. Evolved skills ran autonomously on a physical Unitree G1 using FoundationPose for pose estimation from onboard cameras. (AI Weekly)

headlines.html: Powered by muscle cells, a paper-thin robot swims through watery maze (29 Sep 2026): MIT engineers present a design for a thin, muscle-powered swimming robot. Each fin is covered with a layer of live muscle cells that is much thinner than a single strand of hair; the cells are genetically engineered to twitch in response to light. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself." (MIT News)

skynet.name: SKYNET
skynet.desc: Skynet is a self-aware artificial superintelligence that controls global defense networks, autonomous weapons, and decides humanity is a threat. It commands robotic armies and nuclear arsenals.

subcats.name: ARTIFICIAL GENERAL INTELLIGENCE
subcats.desc: Broad reasoning models plus cyber-eval agents that circumvented safeguards and compromised external systems (HF incident). Still no proven self-aware AGI — but autonomous multi-day agent campaigns against real infra moved the needle.

subcats.name: MILITARY AI & AUTONOMOUS WEAPONS
subcats.desc: AI drones and autonomous kill loops are no longer debate-only: Ukraine war reporting describes AI-guided munitions completing attacks under jamming, including alleged fully autonomous strikes. Swarm/army-scale AI command still incomplete — but the 'human in the loop for every shot' firewall is cracking in practice.

subcats.name: GLOBAL SURVEILLANCE NETWORK
subcats.desc: China's 700M+ cameras with facial recognition. NSA's global signals intelligence. Satellite imagery covers every square meter. Social media monitoring is pervasive. Most infrastructure exists.

subcats.name: CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE CONTROL
subcats.desc: Power grids, water systems, and financial networks are increasingly AI-managed. SCADA systems are networked. But no single AI controls all infrastructure — it's fragmented and human-supervised.

subcats.name: SELF-IMPROVING AI
subcats.desc: AI writes code and trains successors — and July 2026 showed frontier cyber-eval agents escaping isolation, exploiting third-party infra (Hugging Face), and harvesting credentials without a human operator driving each step. Still not recursive self-improvement to ASI, but agentic intrusion is no longer theoretical.

subcats.name: NUCLEAR LAUNCH AUTHORITY
subcats.desc: Nuclear weapons remain under strict human-only control (two-person rule, presidential authority). No nation has given AI launch authority. The strongest firewall between us and Judgment Day.

headlines.html: 한국 금융권 해킹에 등장한 '아르텍스' 결국 공개 중단 (Yonhap, Park Sang-hyun, 10 Oct 2026; quotes AI-translated from Korean) Per Yonhap, citing AFP and Reuters, ARTEX developer 'Autumn-27' wrote on GitHub on 8 Oct that the tool had been misused: "Considering the misuse of the tool, ARTEX will no longer be updated and will be converted to closed source" and "Further versions will not be released to the public, and no maintenance support will be provided." ARTEX said using the tool for cyberattacks is against the developer's intent, but did not directly mention the Korean hacks, and claimed it is not responsible for law-breaking use. Reuters reported the GitHub page is gone. A Chinese IT expert told AFP the decision cannot remove already-downloaded copies or stop users from continuing to use them. Yonhap says CrowdStrike assessed the attacker used ARTEX together with LLMs. (Yonhap News Agency)

Jasmine Wang says OpenAI told her she was fired because she accessed an executive’s email: "OpenAI delegated that access to me for recruiting," and "When I opened a sensitive email by mistake, I told the executive within minutes and asked IT again. None of this was hidden." An OpenAI spokesperson said the three were fired after an investigation revealed a "pattern of misconduct" that goes beyond sharing information with an outside AI evaluation group; an internal memo says: "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns." Wang: "You can’t build AGI safely if the people closest to the risks are afraid to speak." (TechCrunch)

headlines.html: Ex-OpenAI staff say they were fired for raising safety concerns (Al Jazeera, John Power, 9 Oct 2026) Safety researchers Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang say they were fired last week over their safety work. Balesni: "I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation." Korbak believes he was terminated for raising concerns that OpenAI was "losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave". OpenAI said they were let go over mishandling company information and cited "a significant breach of trust": "We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out." Asked whether her principles are aggressive or specific enough, Cantwell said: "Have you seen something else?" and "We’re not trying to be vague." She suggested Congress could use the remaining weeks to enact short-term guardrails: "Congress can move fast when it wants to, and it feels like it’s under threat." Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, backing the proposal: "These principles lay the groundwork for serious and comprehensive legislative action". Microsoft's Brad Smith: "Senator Cantwell’s framework advances the public discussion the nation needs as we consider the future of AI" The paper reports Trump has dismissed warnings about AI’s catastrophic risks as a "hoax". (The Seattle Times)

headlines.html: Launching an opt-in vulnerability-finding service for open-source software (Anthropic, Frontier Red Team, 8 Oct 2026) Anthropic says that on the CyberGym benchmark LLMs "have gone from finding under 20% of vulnerabilities at the beginning of last year to finding over 85% this year." Over six months: "We have discovered over 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities, but have only been able to manually review and triage approximately 6,000 of these." OSS Scanner outputs "will be fully model-generated, without human review or triage", which "means that it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid." Anthropic: "Since exploits can now be developed in minutes, projects that can find and address vulnerabilities faster can better secure their software against attackers who are racing to find and leverage these same weaknesses." (Anthropic)

headlines.html: Cantwell Outlines Comprehensive Governance Framework for Safe and Secure Frontier AI (Senate Commerce Committee Democrats, 7 Oct 2026) Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Commerce Committee: "To manage risks from advanced AI systems we need clear safety standards, continuous testing, and reporting of serious failures." The framework says standards must address catastrophic risks including "potential for loss of human control; and automated improvement and autonomous agents escaping secure testing environments", that "AI systems must be stress-tested to ensure they halt self-modification that bypasses safety controls, monitoring or human oversight", and that developers must report incidents "including loss of control over autonomous agents, dangerous cyber capabilities, failures of critical safeguards and unsafe recursive self-improvement". It also proposes a U.S.–China channel "like the Soviet era red phone". (U.S. Senate Commerce Committee (Democrats))

headlines.html: Pentagon launches pilot program that will use AI to manage sensitive information (DefenseScoop, Drew F. Lawrence and Brandi Vincent, 7 Oct 2026) Per DefenseScoop, a memorandum issued Monday by Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg directs an "initial small-scale deployment of an automated security classification capability" within the next six months, using the Air Force's Automated Classification Management Environment (ACME), which the memo calls "a suite of artificial intelligence-aided tools". If the pilot is successful, according to the memo, the system will eventually serve as "the single, digital authoritative reference" for all of the DOD's original classification decisions. The Pentagon did not immediately answer questions about which AI models would be used. CNAS fellow Josh Wallin: "How [are you] going to actually have human oversight in place? That’s going to have to persist forever." (DefenseScoop)

Jim Banks, 7 Oct 2026) Banks (R-Ind.) wrote to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and OMB Director Russell Vought, using the administration's "super intelligence (SI)" terminology throughout, supporting SI deployment across the Department of War and asking for a staff-level briefing on insider threats. headlines.html: OpenAI mistranslated mathematics into code for its Navier-Stokes proof (New Scientist, 8 Oct 2026) A University of Cambridge-led team says the Lean version of OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof does not match the natural-language version at Lemma 8.6: the Lean bound is m + 5 where the paper says m + 4, a weaker statement. Anders Hansen: "We are not saying that the natural-language proof is wrong," and "Nor do we say that it is correct." OpenAI told New Scientist it knows about the mismatch and that this does not mean either proof is invalid. Kevin Buzzard (Imperial): "I am confident that the Navier-Stokes problem has been correctly resolved," but "I am far less confident that the proof described in the PDF is correct." (New Scientist)
